Requirement: [R.Perceptual-Speed] must function as the ability to quickly and fluently search for and compare similarities or differences in visual stimuli (letters, numbers, patterns, etc.) across an extended visual field. Inputs: [U.V1] (retinotopic visual feature maps; orientation, spatial frequency, color, luminance contrast), [U.V2] (more complex visual features such as contours, textures, stereoscopic disparity), [U.V3] (representations of global motion patterns and dynamic forms), [U.V4] (integrated representations of color constancy and form), [U.MT] (selective representations of visual motion direction and speed), [U.IT] (high-level representations of object categories and forms, identity representations of letters, numbers, and complex patterns), [U.Pulvinar] (fast visual information relay via superior colliculus), [U.FEF] (attention control signals), [U.DLPFC] (search goal templates, task rules, decision criteria). From these inputs, it detects target stimuli in the visual field, computes detection judgment and confidence, and outputs to [U.SC] (saccade targets), [U.PMC] (motor preparation signals), [U.FEF] (attention priority map), [U.DLPFC] (judgment results), [U.V1]-[U.MT] (attention modulation signals). This transformation realizes the entire process of visual search (feature integration → matching selection → judgment), manifesting perceptual speed as a cognitive ability.
Requirement realization by interface: The Interface of [R.Perceptual-Speed] is defined as ([U.SC], [U.PMC], [U.FEF], [U.DLPFC], [U.V1], [U.V2], [U.V3], [U.V4], [U.MT]) = R.Perceptual-Speed([U.V1], [U.V2], [U.V3], [U.V4], [U.MT], [U.IT], [U.Pulvinar], [U.FEF], [U.DLPFC]). The function described in Requirement is fully realized by this Interface. Bottom-up information from visual areas, object information from IT, and fast visual information from Pulvinar are input, and top-down control from FEF and DLPFC is integrated. Outputs include commands to motor systems (SC, PMC), feedback to cognitive control systems (FEF, DLPFC), and modulation to visual systems (V1-MT), encompassing all functions of perceptual speed. This Interface is implemented as hierarchical information processing through child GNs (R.Visual-Integration, R.Goal-Matching-Selection, R.Comparison-Judgment) and their contained UCs (U.pIPS, U.mIPS, U.aIPS).
Capability: The capability to detect and judge target stimuli in the visual field through hierarchical processing of visual information. This capability includes three stages of sequential processing: (1) spatial integration of visual features and priority computation, (2) matching with search goals and selective attention, and (3) evidence accumulation and judgment/confidence evaluation. Each stage combines parallel and sequential processing, integrating bottom-up information and top-down control. This processing is based on computational frameworks such as Priority Map theory (Bisley & Goldberg, 2010), Guided Search 6.0 (Wolfe, 2021), and Drift Diffusion Model (Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008). Perceptual speed is not a single process but an emergent cognitive ability integrating multiple sub-functions. Neuroscientifically, it is implemented as hierarchical information processing in the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) from posterior to middle to anterior (Orban & Caruana, 2014).
Mechanism: Perceptual speed is realized through the following three-stage hierarchical mechanism. Stage 1 (Visual Integration): Parallel inputs from multiple visual areas converge in posterior IPS (pIPS), where bottom-up saliency map and top-down relevance map are integrated to form a priority map. The priority map represents behavioral priority at each spatial location and determines target locations for attention and saccades. Stage 2 (Goal Matching Selection): Based on the priority map, attention spotlights are placed, and middle IPS (mIPS) executes template matching between search goal templates (from DLPFC) and visual information. High-match candidates are selected, while low-match candidates (distractors) are suppressed. Competition is resolved through Winner-take-all mechanism. Stage 3 (Judgment): In anterior IPS (aIPS), evidence is temporally integrated following Drift Diffusion Model, and judgment is finalized when decision threshold (from DLPFC) is reached. Confidence is computed from evidence strength and decision time. Each stage is connected by feedback loops, enabling dynamic adjustment of search.

Requirement: [R.Visual-Integration] must integrate visual information across an extended visual field and construct a searchable representation. Inputs: [U.V1] (retinotopic visual feature maps), [U.V2] (contours, textures), [U.V3] (global motion patterns), [U.V4] (integrated representations of color and form), [U.MT] (visual motion direction and speed), [U.IT] (high-level representations of object categories and forms), [U.Pulvinar] (fast visual information relay), [U.FEF] (attention control signals), [U.DLPFC] (search goal templates). By integrating these, it constructs a spatial priority map across the entire visual field and outputs to [U.mIPS] (input for next-stage selection processing), [U.V1]-[U.MT] (attention-based sensitivity modulation), [U.FEF] (candidate locations for attention shifts). This transformation determines which regions of the visual field should be processed preferentially as the first stage of visual search.
Requirement realization by interface: The Interface of [R.Visual-Integration] is defined as ([U.mIPS], [U.V1], [U.V2], [U.V3], [U.V4], [U.MT], [U.FEF]) = R.Visual-Integration([U.V1], [U.V2], [U.V3], [U.V4], [U.MT], [U.IT], [U.Pulvinar], [U.FEF], [U.DLPFC]). The visual integration function described in Requirement is fully realized by this Interface. Parallel inputs from visual areas converge in [U.pIPS], and additional information from IT and Pulvinar is integrated. Top-down control from FEF and DLPFC emphasizes features related to search goals. Within [U.pIPS], bottom-up saliency and top-down relevance are integrated to form a priority map. This map is sent to [U.mIPS], attention modulation is realized through feedback to visual areas, and attention shifts are controlled through feedback to [U.FEF].
Capability: The capability to spatially integrate information from multiple visual feature channels and construct a behavioral priority map. This capability includes processing to compute local salience of each visual feature (orientation, color, form, motion) using center-surround difference filters and integrate them after normalization. Bottom-up saliency map construction is based on Itti & Koch (2001) Saliency map model. In parallel, similarity between search goal templates and visual features is computed to form a top-down relevance map. Both maps are integrated additively or multiplicatively to generate the final priority map. Priority map is formulated in Bisley & Goldberg (2010) Priority map theory, and it has been demonstrated that LIP neurons additively integrate visual signals, saccadic signals, and cognitive signals (Thomas & Paré, 2007).
Mechanism: Visual integration is realized through the following mechanism. First, visual features are represented retinotopically through parallel projections from each visual area (V1-MT) to [U.pIPS]. Within [U.pIPS], local contrast in each feature channel is computed by center-surround difference, and after normalization, they are integrated to form a bottom-up saliency map. In parallel, similarity between search goal template from [U.DLPFC] and visual representations in [U.pIPS] is computed to form a top-down relevance map. Both maps are integrated (P = α·S_bu + β·S_td) and spatially sharpened through surround suppression. This priority map is dynamically updated, with priority at already-visited locations decreasing through inhibition of return. Peak locations in priority map are sent to [U.mIPS] and [U.FEF] as next attention targets. Simultaneously, feedback projections from [U.pIPS] to visual areas enhance input gain of visual neurons corresponding to high-activity locations in priority map.

Requirement: [R.Goal-Matching-Selection] must match search goals with visual information and select candidates. Inputs: [U.V1]-[U.MT] (visual features), [U.IT] (object representations), [U.Pulvinar] (visual information relay), [U.pIPS] (priority map), [U.FEF] (attention allocation control), [U.DLPFC] (search goal templates, working memory). Based on priority map constructed in [U.pIPS], detailed matching with search goals is executed in [U.mIPS], target candidates are selected, and distractors are suppressed. Selection results are output to [U.aIPS] (input to judgment stage), [U.FEF] (feedback of attention priority map), [U.V1]-[U.MT] (modulation by selective attention). This transformation narrows down candidates with high probability of matching search goals from numerous stimuli in the visual field.
Requirement realization by interface: The Interface of [R.Goal-Matching-Selection] is defined as ([U.aIPS], [U.FEF], [U.V1], [U.V2], [U.V3], [U.V4], [U.MT]) = R.Goal-Matching-Selection([U.V1], [U.V2], [U.V3], [U.V4], [U.MT], [U.IT], [U.Pulvinar], [U.pIPS], [U.FEF], [U.DLPFC]). The matching selection function described in Requirement is realized through cooperation of [U.pIPS] and [U.mIPS]. [U.pIPS] provides priority map, and [U.mIPS] places attention spotlights based on that map. Search goal templates from [U.DLPFC] and visual information from [U.pIPS] are matched in [U.mIPS]. Template matching computes match degree, high-match candidates are selected, and low-match distractors are suppressed. Selection results are sent to [U.aIPS], and attention allocation is continuously adjusted through feedback to [U.FEF]. Processing of selected candidates is emphasized through output to visual areas.
Capability: The capability to match search goal templates with visual information and narrow down candidates through selective attention. This capability includes template matching (similarity computation between visual feature vectors and goal templates) and competitive selection (candidate selection through Winner-take-all mechanism). In Guided Search 6.0 model (Wolfe, 2021), attention spotlights are placed sequentially from high-activity locations in priority map, and each item is processed through diffusion-based recognition process (>150ms/item). Selective attention is adaptively allocated according to target set size and distractor set size (Gillebert et al., 2012). Distractor suppression is realized through pop-in mechanism (sustained suppression after initial enhancement) observed in V4. Feature attention functions as a mechanism to optimize balance between search speed and accuracy (Vater et al., 2023).
Mechanism: Goal matching selection is realized in two stages through [U.pIPS] and [U.mIPS]. Stage 1 ([U.pIPS]): Peak locations in priority map are identified and sent to [U.mIPS] as next attention targets. Stage 2 ([U.mIPS]): Based on priority map from [U.pIPS], attention spotlights are placed sequentially (A(x,y,t) = Θ(P(x,y,t) - θ_att)). Within each spotlight, similarity between visual features (via [U.pIPS]) and search goal template (from [U.DLPFC]) is computed (M_i = sim(V_i, T)). Items exceeding threshold match degree are selected as target candidates and their activity is enhanced. For distractors, sustained suppression is applied after initial enhancement (D_i(t) = max(0, I_i(t) - k·(I_i(t-Δt) + Σ_j w_ij·S_j))). Between multiple candidates, competitive mutual inhibition operates (S_i = M_i·A_i - Σ_{j≠i} w_ij·S_j), and strongest candidate becomes winner. Feature attention strength is adjusted to minimize speed cost and error cost (F = arg min(C_time·RT + C_error·ER)). Selected candidate information is sent to [U.aIPS], and attention allocation state is fed back to [U.FEF].

Requirement: [R.Comparison-Judgment] must judge whether selected candidates match the goal. Inputs: [U.pIPS] (priority map), [U.mIPS] (selected target candidate representations), [U.FEF] (search termination control), [U.DLPFC] (decision criteria, judgment threshold). Candidate information from [U.mIPS] is temporally accumulated in [U.aIPS], compared with judgment threshold to determine presence/absence of target detection. Simultaneously, confidence in judgment is computed. Judgment results are output to [U.pIPS] and [U.mIPS] (feedback whether to continue or terminate search), [U.FEF] and [U.DLPFC] (report of judgment results), [U.SC] and [U.PMC] (initiation of motor response). This transformation finalizes judgment that "target is found" as final stage of visual search and initiates appropriate action.
Requirement realization by interface: The Interface of [R.Comparison-Judgment] is defined as ([U.pIPS], [U.FEF], [U.DLPFC], [U.SC], [U.PMC]) = R.Comparison-Judgment([U.pIPS], [U.mIPS], [U.FEF], [U.DLPFC]). The judgment function described in Requirement is realized through cooperation of [U.mIPS] and [U.aIPS]. [U.mIPS] provides candidate selection information, and [U.aIPS] accumulates that information as evidence. Judgment timing is controlled by judgment threshold from [U.DLPFC]. When evidence reaches threshold, judgment is finalized, and motor response is initiated through output to [U.SC] and [U.PMC]. Simultaneously, confidence is computed and reported to [U.FEF] and [U.DLPFC]. When confidence is low, search continues through feedback to [U.pIPS] and [U.mIPS]. This Interface provides flexible mechanism to adjust speed-accuracy tradeoff in judgment.
Capability: The capability to temporally accumulate sensory evidence and compute binary judgment (target present/absent) and its confidence. This capability includes evidence accumulation process based on Drift Diffusion Model (DDM; Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008). Evidence is accumulated in parallel in two independent integrators representing target hypothesis and no-target hypothesis (dE/dt = μ·S + σ·η(t)). Judgment is finalized when either reaches judgment threshold. Confidence is computed from evidence strength and decision time (Conf ∝ (E_winner - E_loser)/RT). In Bayesian confidence model (Sanders et al., 2016), confidence is defined as posterior probability that judgment is correct. Neuroscientifically, it has been demonstrated that parietal cortex neurons represent confidence as population code (Kiani & Shadlen, 2009). Confidence signal emerges approximately 300ms after stimulus presentation and persists until motor response (Gherman & Philiastides, 2015).
Mechanism: Judgment is realized in two stages through [U.mIPS] and [U.aIPS]. Stage 1 ([U.mIPS]): Match degree of selected candidates is computed and sent to [U.aIPS]. Stage 2 ([U.aIPS]): Evidence from [U.mIPS] is temporally integrated. Two independent integrators (for target-present and target-absent hypotheses) operate in parallel, with increments proportional to evidence drift rate and Gaussian noise added at each time (dE_target/dt = μ_target·S + σ·η(t), dE_notarget/dt = μ_notarget·(1-S) + σ·η(t)). When either integrator reaches judgment threshold set by [U.DLPFC] (θ_decision), judgment is finalized (Choice = arg max(E_target, E_notarget) if max(...) > θ_decision). Decision time is recorded as RT = t (threshold reach time). Confidence is computed as difference between winner and loser integrators divided by decision time (Conf = (E_winner - E_loser)/RT). Alternatively, Bayesian: Conf = P(correct | E, Choice, RT). Evidence accumulation continues after judgment (post-decisional accumulation) and confidence is updated. When confidence is high, judgment result is sent to [U.SC] and [U.PMC] and motor response is initiated. When confidence is low, search continues through feedback to [U.pIPS] and [U.mIPS].
